chapters.title: A Letter to God
chapters.author: G.L. Fuentes
chapters.overview: Lencho, a farmer whose ripe corn is destroyed by a hailstorm, writes a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos. The postmaster, moved by his faith, collects money from his employees and friends and sends a little more than half, signed 'God'. Lencho, sure God cannot make a mistake, writes again asking for the rest and calls the post office employees a bunch of crooks. The chapter also carries two poems by Robert Frost, 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice'.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Poses the question of what we should put our faith in, and invites a guess about whether Lencho's letter reaches God.
Activity on sending money through the post office: discussing words such as counter, acknowledgement and counterfoil, filling out a Money Order form, and completing statements about its parts.

sections.title: A Letter to God
points: Lencho's house sits alone on the crest of a low hill; he hopes for rain for his ripe corn and calls the raindrops 'new coins'.
A strong wind brings large hailstones for an hour; the corn is totally destroyed and the family fears going hungry.
With his one hope in God's help, Lencho writes a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos and posts it.
The postmaster, admiring such faith, collects money from employees and friends and sends a little more than half with a letter signed 'God'.
Lencho, not surprised but angry at the amount, writes that only seventy pesos reached him, asks for the rest, and says not to send it by mail because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: Printed three times during the story (4, 3 and 2 questions).

What Lencho hoped for, why he called raindrops 'new coins', and what happened to his fields; who Lencho had faith in, who read the letter and what the postmaster did; whether Lencho was surprised and what made him angry.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: Who Lencho has complete faith in, and why the postmaster sends the money and signs the letter 'God'.
Whether Lencho tried to find out who sent the money, whom he blames, and the irony of the situation.
What kind of person Lencho is (choosing words such as greedy, naive, unquestioning), and how the conflicts between humans and nature and between humans themselves are illustrated.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise I matches names of storms (gale, whirlwind, cyclone, hurricane, tornado, typhoon) with their descriptions.
Exercise II matches sentences using 'hope' with its meanings.

subsections.title: Relative Clauses
points: Explains non-defining relative clauses beginning with who, whom, whose and which, set off by commas or dashes.
Students join pairs of sentences using the relative pronouns, and note that a relative pronoun can remain 'hidden'.

subsections.title: Using Negatives for Emphasis
points: Shows how words like no, not and nothing can emphasise an idea rather than show absence.
Students find sentences in the story expressing given ideas emphatically with negative words.

subsections.title: Metaphors
points: Explains a metaphor as transferring a quality of one thing to another (the leg of the table, the heart of the city).
In pairs, students complete a table of metaphors from the story: clouds as huge mountains, raindrops, hailstones, locusts, an ox of a man.

sections.title: Speaking
points: Speak in class about a time of great difficulty when only a miracle seemed able to help, and how the problem was solved.

sections.title: Listening
points: Listen to a letter read out by the teacher (printed under 'In This Lesson') and fill in a table: why the writer apologises, what she has sent, the reason for not writing earlier, and who is writing to whom.

sections.title: Writing
points: Design a poster for your area on how to save water during summer and when it is available in excess, after Lencho's drought and floods.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Notes for the teacher under 'What We Have Done' and 'What You Can Do'.
Gives the letter from Jaya to Arti used for the listening activity, and suggestions for reading, grammar and speaking.

sections.title: Dust of Snow
points: A poem by Robert Frost: a crow shaking down dust of snow from a hemlock tree changes the poet's mood and saves part of a day he had rued.
Presents a simple moment with a larger significance.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: On 'Dust of Snow': what a 'dust of snow' is and what changed the poet's mood.
How Frost presents nature through the crow and the hemlock, and what they represent.
Whether you have experienced a similar moment that changed your mood.

sections.title: Fire and Ice
points: A poem by Robert Frost on whether the world will end in fire or in ice.
From desire he holds with fire, but from what he knows of hate, ice would also suffice for destruction.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: On 'Fire and Ice': ideas about how the world will end.
What 'fire' and 'ice' stand for, choosing from ideas such as greed, hatred, intolerance and coldness.
The rhyme scheme of the poem and how it brings out the contrasting ideas.

keyTerms.meaning: insects which fly in big swarms (groups) and destroy crops
currency of several Latin American countries
an inner sense of right and wrong
A poisonous plant (tree) with small white flowers
a comparison of two things or ideas in which a quality or feature of one thing is transferred to another

keyResults.label: Character: Lencho
keyResults.statement: A farmer, 'an ox of a man', who knows how to write and has complete faith in God.

keyResults.label: Character: The postmaster
keyResults.statement: A fat, amiable fellow who answers Lencho's letter so as not to shake his faith in God.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: Faith — and the irony that Lencho suspects the very people who helped him.

keyResults.label: Literary device: irony
keyResults.statement: The book defines an ironic situation as one that is the opposite of what is expected, as when Lencho calls his helpers crooks.

keyResults.label: Literary device: metaphor
keyResults.statement: The story compares clouds to huge mountains, hailstones to new silver coins, and Lencho to an ox.

keyResults.label: Poetic device: rhyme scheme
keyResults.statement: 'Fire and Ice' asks how its rhyme scheme brings out the poem's contrasting ideas.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the writer's name 'G.L.Fuentes' under the title, and the picture headings Thinking about the Text, Thinking about Language, Speaking, Listening, Writing, In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem (after each poem). Some of these words also occur in the extracted body text (the teacher's notes mention 'Thinking about the Text'), but the headings themselves are pictures. Each poem also has a pictured 'Glossary' heading, whose words are under keyTerms. Relative Clauses, Using Negatives for Emphasis and Metaphors are exercises III–V inside Thinking about Language.

chapters.title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
chapters.author: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela
chapters.overview: In this extract from his autobiography, Nelson Mandela describes his inauguration on 10 May 1994 as South Africa's first black President, attended by leaders of many nations, and reflects on the long struggle against apartheid. He writes about courage as triumph over fear, about the twin obligations to family and to one's people, and about how his hunger for his own freedom became a hunger for the freedom of his people. He concludes that the oppressor, like the oppressed, is robbed of humanity. The chapter ends with the poem 'A Tiger in the Zoo' by Leslie Norris.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Explains apartheid as a political system separating people by race, and asks which country had it.
Introduces Mandela, his thirty years in prison and the 1994 elections, with a BBC news item on his becoming South Africa's first black President.
Activity: matching expressions from the text (a rainbow gathering, a twilight existence, etc.) with their meanings.

sections.title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
points: The inauguration takes place in the sandstone amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, once the seat of white supremacy; de Klerk and Thabo Mbeki are sworn in as deputy presidents.
Mandela's speech pledges to liberate all people from poverty, deprivation and discrimination: 'Never, never, and never again...'
Jets fly past, generals salute him, and the two national anthems are sung, symbolising the day.
He reflects that apartheid produced men of extraordinary courage such as Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu, and that courage is the triumph over fear, not its absence.
He describes the twin obligations to family and to people, and how his boyhood freedom proved an illusion.
His hunger for his own freedom became the greater hunger for the freedom of his people; the oppressor must be liberated as surely as the oppressed.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: Printed three times during the text (5, 5 and 3 questions).
Where the ceremonies took place, why 10 May is an autumn day, the 'human disaster' and 'glorious achievement', and the ideals Mandela sets out.
What the generals do, why two anthems were sung, and what courage means to Mandela.
The 'twin obligations', what freedom meant to him at different ages, and whether the oppressor is free.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: Why so many international leaders attended the inauguration and what it signified the triumph of.
What Mandela means by being 'the sum of all those African patriots', and whether the 'depths of oppression' create 'heights of character'.
How Mandela's understanding of freedom changed with age and experience, and how his 'hunger for freedom' changed his life.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise I lists noun–verb pairs formed with -(at)ion or -ment and fills in noun forms in a paragraph on Martin Luther King.

subsections.title: Using the Definite Article with Names
points: Explains that 'the' with a plural proper noun (the Oliver Tambos) means men of that kind.
Students explain sentences such as 'the Madhubala of our times'.

subsections.title: Idiomatic Expressions
points: Matching phrases such as 'not unmindful of', 'pushed to our limits', 'keep me going' and 'earning my keep' with their meanings.

sections.title: Speaking
points: In groups, discuss poverty, discrimination and constitutional rights, then prepare a two-minute speech on 'True liberty is freedom from poverty, deprivation and all forms of discrimination.'

sections.title: Writing
points: Exercise II finds the second half of contrasts between the past and the present or future in the text.

subsections.title: Looking at Contrasts
points: Mandela's sentences have two balanced parts; students complete contrasts such as 'courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it'.

subsections.title: Expressing Your Opinion
points: A paragraph of 100 to 150 words on whether there is colour prejudice in our country, optionally humorous, with a short verse as a model.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes: research in groups on black Americans, women and the Vietnamese and their fights for equality and independence.

sections.title: Homophones
points: Words spelt alike with different meanings: wound/wound, desert/dessert/desert.

sections.title: A Tiger in the Zoo
points: A poem by Leslie Norris contrasting a tiger stalking the few steps of his cage with the tiger in its natural habitat.
He should be lurking in shadow near the water hole or terrorising the village, but is locked in a concrete cell, ignoring visitors, staring at the stars.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: Find words describing the tiger's movements and the two places, in the cage and in the wild.
The effect of repeated words ('quiet', 'brilliant').
Discuss whether zoos are necessary, after reading 'The Tiger' by Peter Niblett and 'The Panther' by Rainer Maria Rilke; then write or speak for or against zoos.
'The Greater Cats' by Victoria Sackville-West is also printed.

keyTerms.meaning: a building without a roof, with many rows of seats rising in steps (typical of ancient Greece and Rome)
state of not having one's rightful benefits
a pattern in the shape of a V
the ability to deal with any kind of hardship and recover from its effects
something that appears to be real but is not
a strong dislike without any good reason
a political system that separates people according to their race
a half-secret life, like a life lived in the fading light between sunset and darkness

keyResults.label: Character: Nelson Mandela
keyResults.statement: Leader of the African National Congress who spent thirty years in prison and became South Africa's first black President in 1994.

keyResults.label: Theme: courage
keyResults.statement: Courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it.

keyResults.label: Theme: freedom
keyResults.statement: Freedom is indivisible; the oppressed and the oppressor alike are robbed of their humanity.

keyResults.label: Theme: love and hate
keyResults.statement: No one is born hating; people learn to hate and can be taught to love, which comes more naturally to the human heart.

keyResults.label: Style: contrasts
keyResults.statement: Mandela's writing is marked by balance, with many sentences contrasting the past with the present or future.

keyResults.label: Poetic device: repetition
keyResults.statement: 'A Tiger in the Zoo' repeats words such as 'quiet' and 'brilliant', and the book asks about their effect.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the writer's name 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela' under the title, and the picture headings Thinking about the Text, Thinking about Language, Speaking, Writing, In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem, plus a pictured 'Glossary' heading before the poem questions. Using the Definite Article with Names and Idiomatic Expressions are exercises II and III of Thinking about Language; Looking at Contrasts and Expressing Your Opinion are exercises I and III of Writing.

chapters.title: Two Stories about Flying
chapters.author: Liam O'Flaherty, Frederick Forsyth
chapters.overview: Two stories about flying. In 'His First Flight' by Liam O'Flaherty a young seagull, afraid to fly, is made to dive by hunger when his mother holds food just out of reach, and finds he can fly. In 'The Black Aeroplane' by Frederick Forsyth a pilot flying his Dakota home takes the risk of flying into a storm, loses his instruments, and is guided to an airport by a mysterious black aeroplane that no one else saw. The chapter also carries the poems 'How to Tell Wild Animals' by Carolyn Wells and 'The Ball Poem' by John Berryman.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Humans have long dreamt of conquering the skies; introduces a young seagull afraid to fly and a pilot lost in storm clouds.

sections.title: His First Flight
points: By Liam O'Flaherty.
The young seagull is alone on his ledge, afraid to fly though his brothers and sister have flown; his parents scold and threaten to let him starve.
Hungry, he watches his family and begs his mother for food; she flies towards him with fish but stops just out of reach.
Maddened by hunger he dives at the fish, falls, and finds his wings spread and carry him.
He flies over the sea, lands on the water, floats, and his family praises him: he has made his first flight.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: Why the young seagull was afraid to fly, what compelled him to fly, and why his parents threatened and cajoled him.
Experiences of being encouraged to try something you were too scared to try, and whether success is guaranteed or trying matters regardless.

sections.title: Speaking
points: Group presentations on topics such as the progression of models of airplanes and motorcars, birds and their wing span, and migratory birds.

sections.title: Writing
points: A short, humorous composition on your initial attempts at learning a skill, such as riding a bicycle or swimming.

sections.title: The Black Aeroplane
points: By Frederick Forsyth.
The narrator flies his old Dakota over France to England at night, dreaming of breakfast with his family.
Facing huge storm clouds and short of fuel, he decides 'I'll take the risk' and flies into the storm.
His compass, instruments and radio die; a black aeroplane without lights appears and its pilot signals him to follow.
He follows it down to a runway and lands safely, but the black aeroplane has vanished.
The woman in the control centre says no other aeroplane was flying that night; the narrator wonders who helped him.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: What the risk is and why the narrator takes it; his experience flying into the storm.
Why he was not sorry to walk away from the old Dakota, why the woman looked at him strangely, and who might have helped him.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise I studies the different meanings of 'black' in context (a black look, black comedy, sold in black) and guesses them before checking a dictionary.
Exercise II matches phrases with 'fly' (fly a flag, fly into a rage, fly high, fly the coop) with their meanings.
Exercise III ticks words with the same or nearly the same meaning as 'fly' (swoop, flit, hover, glide ...).

sections.title: Writing
points: Narrate in a paragraph an experience of being alone or away from home during a thunderstorm.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes: comparing a baby learning to walk with the seagull, discussing the phantom plane, and students narrating their own stories about flying.

sections.title: Compound Words Whose Parts Mean Just the Opposite or Something Else
points: A box of examples: quicksand works slowly; there is no egg in eggplant nor ham in hamburger; boxing rings are square.

sections.title: How to Tell Wild Animals
points: A humorous poem by Carolyn Wells suggesting dangerous ways to identify wild animals: the Asian Lion roars as you are dying, the Bengal Tiger eats you, the Leopard leaps on you.
A Bear hugs you very hard, a Crocodile weeps while a Hyena smiles, and a Chameleon is identified when nothing is seen on the tree.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: Whether 'dyin'' rhymes with 'lion', and how the poet suggests identifying the lion and the tiger.
The spellings 'lept' and 'lep', the 'bearhug' and 'crocodile tears', and the 'incorrect' line 'A novice might nonplus'.
Poets taking liberties with language, and sharing lines whose humour comes from the language or the ideas.

sections.title: English is funny, because…
points: A box: we have noses that run and feet that smell.

sections.title: The Ball Poem
points: A poem by John Berryman about a boy who loses his ball in the harbour and is gripped by grief.
The poet will not intrude or offer money for another ball; the boy is learning responsibility in a world of possessions and 'the epistemology of loss'.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: In pairs: why the poet does not intrude, whether the boy had the ball a long time, and what 'in the world of possessions' means.
Whether the boy has lost anything earlier, what he is learning from the loss, and a paragraph on losing something you liked very much.

keyTerms.meaning: a narrow horizontal shelf projecting from a wall or (here) a cliff
to move lightly just above a surface (here, the sea)
in a manner showing someone that she/he is stupid
making an effort to maintain feathers
flying with one wing higher than the other
here, to enter a situation where one is not welcome
understanding the nature of loss — what it means to lose something

keyResults.label: Character: The young seagull
keyResults.statement: A young bird afraid to fly who conquers his fear when hunger makes him dive for food.

keyResults.label: Character: The narrator (pilot)
keyResults.statement: A pilot flying his old Dakota home who takes the risk of flying into a storm and is guided to safety.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: Overcoming fear and taking risks; the second story leaves the identity of the helping pilot a mystery.

keyResults.label: Poetic device: poetic licence
keyResults.statement: 'How to Tell Wild Animals' uses 'incorrect' spellings and word order ('lept', 'lep', 'A novice might nonplus') for rhyme and humour.

keyResults.label: Theme of 'The Ball Poem'
keyResults.statement: Learning to bear loss and to stand up, knowing what every man must one day know.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the writers 'Liam O' Flaherty' (I. His First Flight) and 'Frederick Forsyth' (II. Black Aeroplane, so titled on the opening page and 'The Black Aeroplane' above the story), and the picture headings Thinking about the Text (after each story), Speaking, Writing (after each story), Thinking about Language, In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem (after each poem), plus pictured 'Glossary' headings. 'Study the sentences given below' is the instruction opening Thinking about Language exercise I, not a heading, and has been removed. This chapter has no Oral Comprehension Check.

chapters.title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
chapters.author: Anne Frank
chapters.overview: Extracts from the diary of Anne Frank, a thirteen-year-old Jewish girl. She explains why she keeps a diary — she has no true friend — and names it 'Kitty', gives a brief sketch of her family and life, and describes how her maths teacher Mr Keesing punished her for talking in class with essays, until her poem 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox' won him over. The chapter ends with the poem 'Amanda!' by Robin Klein.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Introduces Anne Frank, who hid with her family in Amsterdam during the German occupation, died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen, and whose diary her father had published as The Diary of a Young Girl.
Activity: matching journal, diary, log and memoir(s) with their descriptions, and deciding which personal records are which.

sections.title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
points: Anne finds writing a diary strange but feels 'Paper has more patience than people'; she has family and about thirty friends but no true friend, so the diary will be her friend 'Kitty'.
She sketches her life: born 12 June 1929 in Frankfurt, moved to Holland, Montessori school, her teacher Mrs Kuperus, and her grandmother's death in January 1942.
In the entry of 20 June 1942 the class is nervous about promotion; Mr Keesing, the maths teacher, gives her an essay on 'A Chatterbox' for talking.
She argues talking is a student's trait inherited from her mother; further essays follow, including 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'.
She writes it as a poem with her friend Sanne's help; Mr Keesing takes the joke well, reads it to classes, and lets her talk.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: Printed three times during the text (3, 2 and 4 questions).

Why writing a diary is strange for Anne and why she keeps one; why she gives a sketch of her life and loves her grandmother; why Mr Keesing was annoyed, whether he was strict, and what made him allow her to talk.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: Whether the world would be interested in a thirteen-year-old's musings, and how Anne's diary differs from the entries in 'Before You Read'.
Why she sketches her family, how she feels about her father, grandmother, Mrs Kuperus and Mr Keesing, and what she wrote in her first essay.
Whether Mr Keesing is unpredictable, and what given statements tell us about Anne as a person.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise I explains compound words (headmistress, long-awaited) and matches compounds with meanings.
Exercise IV shows how to find idiomatic expressions in a dictionary, with an entry for 'eye', and expressions with 'heart'.

subsections.title: Phrasal Verbs
points: Explains phrasal verbs whose meaning differs from their parts; students look up and match plunge in, kept back, ramble on, get along with, make up for, hand in and others.

subsections.title: Idioms
points: Explains idioms as fixed groups of words with special meanings; students explain 'quaking in its boots', 'lose heart', 'for ages' and use 'caught my eye', 'laugh ourselves silly' in sentences.

subsections.title: Contracted Forms
points: Explains contracted forms (can't, I'd, she's) used in diaries, plays and novels; students list them and find those standing for two different full forms.

sections.title: Speaking
points: A play extract about Joe the Inventor's neighbours is rewritten with contracted forms and spoken aloud.

sections.title: Writing
points: Keep a diary for a week, using features of 'diary language' such as subjectless sentences, fragments and contracted forms.

sections.title: Listening
points: Listen to an extract from The Diary of Samuel Pepys about the Great Fire of London and complete a summary.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes on diary writing and diaries that became historical documents.
Prints the listening passage 'The Great Fire of London [1666]' from The Diary of Samuel Pepys.

sections.title: Amanda!
points: A poem by Robin Klein in which a girl, Amanda, is constantly instructed and scolded ('Don't bite your nails, Amanda!').
In stanzas in parenthesis she imagines being a mermaid, an orphan roaming the street, and Rapunzel in a tower, free and untroubled.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: Amanda's age, who is speaking to her, and why stanzas 2, 4 and 6 are in parenthesis.
What she could do as a mermaid, whether she is an orphan, why she wants to be Rapunzel, what she yearns for, and whether she is sulking and moody.

keyTerms.meaning: to tell personal things privately to a person that one trusts
put down in a casual way
talk or write aimlessly for long
something that cannot be corrected (usually a bad quality)
qualities (physical or mental) that one gets from one's parents

keyResults.label: Character: Anne Frank
keyResults.statement: A thirteen-year-old schoolgirl who keeps a diary she calls 'Kitty' because she has no true friend.

keyResults.label: Character: Mr Keesing
keyResults.statement: Anne's old-fashioned maths teacher who punishes her talking with essays and finally takes her poem as a joke.

keyResults.label: Character: Margot
keyResults.statement: Anne's elder sister, born in Frankfurt in 1926.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: A diary as a trusted friend; Anne's wit and originality turn a punishment into a joke on the teacher.

keyResults.label: Character (poem): Amanda
keyResults.statement: A girl who escapes constant instructions by imagining freedom as a mermaid, an orphan and Rapunzel.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the writer's name 'Anne Frank' under the title, and the picture headings Thinking about the Text, Thinking about Language, Speaking, Writing, Listening, In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem, plus a pictured 'Glossary' heading. Phrasal Verbs, Idioms and Contracted Forms are exercises II, III and V of Thinking about Language.

chapters.title: Glimpses of India
chapters.author: Lucio Rodrigues, Lokesh Abrol, Arup Kumar Datta
chapters.overview: Three pieces giving glimpses of different regions of India: a pen-portrait of the traditional Goan village baker (pader) and his place in society by Lucio Rodrigues, a description of Coorg, the coffee country of Karnataka with its martial people and rainforests, by Lokesh Abrol, and Arup Kumar Datta's story of Rajvir's visit to a tea estate in Assam with his friend Pranjol. The chapter ends with the poem 'The Trees' by Adrienne Rich.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Activity to discuss in class: images of India, places visited, parts showing French and Portuguese influences, and where tea and coffee are grown.

sections.title: A Baker from Goa
points: By Lucio Rodrigues.
Elders in Goa recall the Portuguese days and their loaves; the bakers, called pader, still carry on the family profession.
In the author's childhood the baker came twice a day with the 'jhang, jhang' of his bamboo; children longed for bread-bangles.
Bread is essential in Goan life: the sweet bread bol for marriage gifts, sandwiches for engagements, cakes and bolinhas for Christmas.
The baker wore a knee-length frock called the kabai; bills were recorded on a wall and collected monthly; bakers looked plump and prosperous.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: Printed twice (4 and 5 questions).

What the elders are nostalgic about, what the baker is called and when he came; matching bread items to occasions, the baker's dress, where his accounts were recorded, and what a 'jackfruit-like appearance' means.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: Which statements about paders are correct, and whether bread is an important part of Goan life.
The tone of the author (nostalgic, hopeful, sad, naughty, funny, matter-of-fact) in given lines.

sections.title: Writing
points: Exercise I completes a table on bread-baking in the author's childhood and writes a paragraph about it.
Exercise II compares the text with another piece on Goan paders, and writes a personal account of a place after reading a travel brochure.

sections.title: Group Discussion
points: Collect information on how bakeries bake bread now, and make a group presentation on a dying craft-based profession such as pottery, batik work or bamboo weaving.

sections.title: Coorg
points: By Lokesh Abrol.
Coorg (Kodagu), the smallest district of Karnataka between Mysore and Mangalore, has evergreen rainforests, spices and coffee plantations.
Its people may be of Greek or Arabic descent; the kuppia coat resembles the Arab kuffia; the Coorg Regiment is among the most decorated and General Cariappa was a Coorgi.
Kodavus are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence.
The Kaveri gets its water here; visitors enjoy rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing, trekking, the Brahmagiri hills, Nisargadhama and the Tibetan settlement at Bylakuppe.

subsections.title: Fact File
points: How to Reach: Madikeri is the gateway to Coorg, by air via Mangalore or Bangalore, by rail via Mysore, Mangalore or Hassan, and by road from Bangalore.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: Where Coorg is and the story of the Kodavu people's descent.
What we now know about the people, main crop, sports, animals and distance of Coorg, and phrases in the text matching given italicised words.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Language work on the Coorg piece.

subsections.title: Collocations
points: Explains collocations as words that 'go together'; students pair nouns (culture, monks, surprise, experience, weather, tradition) with adjectives and complete phrases from the text.

sections.title: Tea from Assam
points: By Arup Kumar Datta.
Pranjol and Rajvir travel by train to Assam; Rajvir notes that over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk daily worldwide.
Rajvir tells legends of tea's discovery: the Chinese emperor whose boiling water received tea leaves, and Bodhidharma, whose cut eyelids grew tea plants.
Tea was first drunk in China as far back as 2700 B.C. and reached Europe in the sixteenth century.
At Dhekiabari Tea Estate, managed by Pranjol's father Mr Barua, they see tea-pluckers; Rajvir knows the second-flush period, May to July, yields the best tea.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise I uses words built from a verb and a particle (upkeep, downpour, undergo, dropout, walk-in) and forms such words from verbs in brackets.
Exercise II explains -ing and -ed adjectives and uses them to describe experiences and to write a paragraph about Coorg.

sections.title: Speaking and Writing
points: Read a passage on tea, collect information about it, and play the roles of a tea planter, sales agent, tea lover, physician and tea-shop owner.
Draft an advertisement for a tea company using the information collected.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes: an exhibition of photographs of different places in India, with write-ups, discussion and a vote.

sections.title: The Trees
points: A poem by Adrienne Rich in which trees kept inside a house move out into an empty forest during the night.
Roots work free of the veranda floor, leaves strain toward the glass, and boughs shuffle like newly discharged patients.
The poet writes letters that scarcely mention the forest's departure; the glass breaks and the moon is broken like a mirror.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: What cannot happen in a treeless forest, what the sun's 'feet' might be, and what the branches are compared to.
How the moon is described, what happens to the house, and why the poet does not mention the forest's departure in her letters.
Whether the poem presents a conflict between man and nature (compared with 'A Tiger in the Zoo') or uses trees as a metaphor for human beings; comparison with 'On Killing a Tree' by Gieve Patel.

sections.title: Homophones
points: Words spelt alike with different meanings: refuse/refuse, dove/dove, invalid/invalid.

keyTerms.meaning: an expression of disapproval; a scolding
public statement about a character or quality
the name by which traditional bakers are known in Goa
the baker's peculiar dress, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees
stories of courage and bravery, usually in war
having received the maximum number of awards for bravery in war
going down a cliff by sliding down a rope
a view of a wide area of land
crusty patches or bushy growth on tree trunks/bare ground formed by association of fungus and alga

keyResults.label: Character: The pader
keyResults.statement: The traditional Goan village baker, once the children's friend, companion and guide, who still has an important place in his society.

keyResults.label: Character: Rajvir
keyResults.statement: A Delhi schoolboy who has read up on tea and visits his classmate's tea estate in Assam.

keyResults.label: Character: Pranjol
keyResults.statement: Rajvir's classmate, son of Mr Barua, manager of Dhekiabari Tea Estate in Upper Assam.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: How varied, charming and beautiful India is, seen through three regions.

keyResults.label: Poetic device: metaphor
keyResults.statement: The book notes that Adrienne Rich uses trees as a metaphor for human beings.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the writers 'Lucio Rodrigues' (I. A Baker from Goa), 'Lokesh Abrol' (II. Coorg) and 'Arup Kumar Datta' (III. Tea from Assam), listed on the opening page, and the picture headings Thinking about the Text (after I and II), Writing, Group Discussion, Thinking about Language (after II and III), Speaking and Writing, In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem, plus a pictured 'Glossary' heading. Collocations is a printed sub-heading inside the Coorg piece's Thinking about Language. 'Tea from Assam' has no Oral Comprehension Check or Thinking about the Text. The Coorg piece includes a printed 'Fact File' box headed 'How to Reach'.

chapters.title: Mijbil the Otter
chapters.author: Gavin Maxwell
chapters.overview: Gavin Maxwell, who lives at Camusfearna in Scotland, decides to keep an otter instead of a dog and gets one in Southern Iraq. The otter, Mijbil, turns out to be of a race unknown to science and is named Maxwell's otter. Maxwell describes Mij's love of water and play, the drama of flying him to London in a box, and the strange guesses Londoners make about what animal he is. The chapter ends with the poem 'Fog' by Carl Sandburg.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Maxwell, sad after his dog Jonnie died, finds life without a pet lonely.
Activity: the SPCA's advice on the responsibility of owning a pet, a list of what to know about a gifted pet, and planning to bring an otter from Iraq to London using information on both places.

sections.title: Mijbil the Otter
points: In 1956 Maxwell travels to Southern Iraq, thinking Camusfearna suitable for keeping an otter; a friend advises getting one in the Tigris marshes.
At Basra he waits for his delayed mail; when it arrives, two Arabs bring a sack with an otter sent by his friend.

sections.title: Mijbil the Otter
points: The mud-coated otter resembles a small medievally-conceived dragon; named Mijbil, he is of a race unknown to science, christened Maxwell's otter.
At first aloof and indifferent, he soon sleeps on Maxwell's bed and goes wild with joy in the bathtub, learning to turn on the tap.
He follows Maxwell without a lead, plays with a rubber ball and juggles marbles on his belly.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: After parts I and II (6 questions): the experiment Maxwell planned, why he went to Basra, how he got the otter, why it was named Maxwell's otter, how it behaved at first, and what happened in the bathroom.

sections.title: Mijbil the Otter
points: The airline requires Mij to travel in a box; he tears its lining and is found blood-spattered.
On the flight to Paris a kind air hostess lets Mij sit on Maxwell's knee; Mij escapes, causes screams and returns to nuzzle Maxwell.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: After part III (5 questions): how Mij was transported, what he did to the box, why Maxwell put him back in it, why the air hostess was 'the very queen of her kind', and what happened when the box was opened.

sections.title: Mijbil the Otter
points: In London Mij invents a game with a ping-pong ball on a sloping suitcase.
On walks he develops compulsive habits, such as galloping along a school wall on the way home.
Londoners guess he is a baby seal, squirrel, walrus, hippo, beaver or brontosaur; a labourer asks, 'what is that supposed to be?'

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: After part IV (4 questions): Mij's game, compulsive habits of school children and of Mij, the group of animals otters belong to, and Londoners' guesses.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: What shows Mij is intelligent, friendly and fun-loving, what we learn about otters, and why the species is called Maxwell's otter.
What Maxwell says Mij feels and thinks, and sentences illustrating statements about Maxwell's description of his pet.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise III covers phrases of quantity such as a cloud of dust, a pinch of salt, a bit of advice.

subsections.title: Describing a Repeated Action in the Past
points: Explains 'would' and 'used to' for repeated past actions, and 'used to' alone for past states; students make sentences from a table.

subsections.title: Noun Modifiers
points: Explains nouns, proper nouns and adjectival phrases used as noun modifiers (the Christmas dinner party); students classify examples and combine nouns and modifiers from the book.

sections.title: Speaking
points: Play dumb charades, expressing a feeling or thought silently through gestures while the class guesses.

sections.title: Writing
points: Describe a person or animal (such as a pet) you know well and love, saying what they do, feel and think.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes: changes over half a century in keeping pets and transporting animals, the ethics of keeping wild animals as pets, and otter conservation.

sections.title: Fog
points: A poem by Carl Sandburg: the fog comes on little cat feet, sits looking over harbour and city on silent haunches, and moves on.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: What the fog is like, how it comes, and three things that tell us it is like a cat.
Finding metaphors for storm, train, fire, school and home, and writing a poem comparing a storm with an animal.
Whether the poem has a rhyme scheme; poetry without obvious rhythm or rhyme is 'free verse'.

keyTerms.meaning: a very strong attachment or feeling
a bullet which changes direction after hitting a surface
to rub gently with the nose
a stream of questions filled with guesses
poetry that does not have an obvious rhythm or rhyme

keyResults.label: Character: Gavin Maxwell
keyResults.statement: The narrator, living at Camusfearna in the West Highlands of Scotland, who brings an otter from Iraq.

keyResults.label: Character: Mijbil (Mij)
keyResults.statement: An otter of a race previously unknown to science, named Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli, or Maxwell's otter; playful and fond of water.

keyResults.label: Character: The air hostess
keyResults.statement: The helpful hostess Maxwell calls 'the very queen of her kind'.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: The bond between a man and an unusual pet, observed closely and with humour.

keyResults.label: Poetic device: metaphor
keyResults.statement: 'Fog' compares the fog to a cat without saying so directly.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the writer's name 'Gavin Maxwell' under the title, and the picture headings Thinking about the Text, Thinking about Language, Speaking, Writing, In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem, plus a pictured 'Glossary' heading. Parts I–IV are printed with numerals only, so each is given the chapter title. The Oral Comprehension Checks come after part II, part III and part IV. Describing a Repeated Action in the Past and Noun Modifiers are exercises I and II of Thinking about Language.

chapters.title: Madam Rides the Bus
chapters.author: Vallikkannan
chapters.overview: Valli, an eight-year-old village girl, longs to ride the bus to the nearby town. She secretly saves sixty paise and plans the trip for her mother's afternoon nap, rides to the town and back, and enjoys the sights and the joking conductor who calls her 'madam'. On the way back she sees a cow she had laughed at lying dead on the road, and her first journey becomes an induction into the mystery of death. The chapter ends with the poem 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon' by Ogden Nash.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: An eight-year-old girl's first bus journey is also her induction into the mystery of life and death.
Activity: ticking words and phrases likely in the text, and speaking about scenes seen from a moving bus.

sections.title: Madam Rides the Bus
points: Valliammai (Valli) loves watching the street from her doorway, especially the bus to town.
She longs to ride it and learns details: the town is six miles away, the fare thirty paise each way, and the trip forty-five minutes.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: After part I (4 questions): Valli's favourite pastime, her strongest desire, what she found out about the bus journey and how, and what she was planning.

sections.title: Madam Rides the Bus
points: Valli stops the bus, refuses help getting on, and the jolly conductor calls her 'madam'.
She stands on the seat to see the canal, palm trees and fields, and tells an elderly man she is not a child.
She finds an elderly woman chewing betel repulsive and refuses to be friendly.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: After part II (4 questions): why the conductor calls Valli 'madam', why she stands on the seat, what she tells the elderly man, and why she would not befriend the elderly woman.

sections.title: Madam Rides the Bus
points: She had saved sixty paise, resisting even the merry-go-round, and slipped out during her mother's nap.
She laughs at a young cow running in front of the bus, sees a train and the town's shops.
At the town she stays on for the return trip and refuses the conductor's offer of a cold drink.

sections.title: Oral Comprehension Check
points: After part III (4 questions): how Valli saved money, what made her laugh, why she did not get off at the bus station, and why she refused a drink.

sections.title: Madam Rides the Bus
points: On the way back she sees the same cow lying dead by the road and is overcome with sadness, no longer wanting to look out.
Home by three forty, she hears her mother say we often cannot understand things completely, and agrees, smiling to herself.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: Valli's deepest desire, how she planned the ride, and what kind of person she is (completing sentences from the text).
Why the conductor calls her 'madam', lines showing her enjoyment, why she refuses to look out on the way back, and what she means by agreeing with her mother.
Evidence that the sights are described from an eight-year-old's point of view.

sections.title: Speaking
points: Recall similar people or situations from the story's many conversations and mimic what they said, with your replies.

sections.title: Writing
points: Write a page on one of three topics: planning something on your own, an unforgettable journey, or traffic and road safety.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes: a collage of collected used tickets, and pair and group discussions on pocket money and on a troubling incident.

sections.title: The Tale of Custard the Dragon
points: A humorous ballad, close to a parody, by Ogden Nash about Belinda and her pets Ink the kitten, Blink the mouse, Mustard the dog and Custard, a cowardly dragon.
The others laugh at Custard for crying for a nice safe cage.
When a pirate climbs in, the brave pets flee, but Custard attacks and gobbles up the pirate.
Afterwards the others claim they would have been braver, Custard agrees everyone is braver than him, and he keeps crying for a safe cage.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: The characters and their pet names, why Custard cried for a safe cage, and why Belinda tickled him.
Poetic devices such as simile, the description of the dragon, the rhyme scheme and images.
Whether the poem is serious or light-hearted, and collecting modern songs that tell a story.

sections.title: Writing
points: Write your own ballad, following guidelines on purpose, audience, narrative, characters, rhythm, rhyme, refrain and verses.

keyTerms.meaning: informal words, often used within a close group
a time when there is not much work
returned repeatedly to her mind; was impossible to forget
a song or poem that tells a story
a drink typically drunk by sailors

keyResults.label: Character: Valli (Valliammai)
keyResults.statement: A curious, independent, determined eight-year-old who plans and makes her first bus journey on her own.

keyResults.label: Character: The conductor
keyResults.statement: A jolly man fond of joking who calls Valli 'madam'.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: The gap between knowing that there is death and understanding it.

keyResults.label: Point of view
keyResults.statement: The book asks students to find evidence that the sights are described from an eight-year-old's point of view.

keyResults.label: Poetic device: simile
keyResults.statement: 'Clashed his tail like irons in a dungeon' is given as a simile in 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon'.

keyResults.label: Form of the poem
keyResults.statement: 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon' is a humorous ballad close to a parody.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the writer's name 'Vallikkannan' under the title (the story ends '[Translated from the Tamil by K. S. Sundaram / Illustrated by R. K. Laxman]'), and the picture headings Thinking about the Text, Speaking, Writing (after the story and after the poem), In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem, plus a pictured 'Glossary' heading. Parts I–IV are printed with numerals only, so each is given the chapter title. The Oral Comprehension Checks come after parts I, II and III; there is no Thinking about Language in this chapter.

chapters.title: The Sermon at Benares
chapters.overview: After an account of how Prince Siddhartha Gautama became the Buddha, the chapter gives his first sermon at Benares. Kisa Gotami, grieving for her dead son, is told by the Buddha to bring mustard seed from a house where no one has died; she finds none, and realises death is common to all and that she was selfish in her grief. The Buddha teaches that the wise do not grieve and that peace comes from drawing out the arrow of lamentation. The chapter ends with the poem 'For Anne Gregory' by W.B. Yeats.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Activity: what a sermon is, meanings of words such as afflicted with, desolation and lamentation, and the Sermon on the Mount.

sections.title: The Sermon at Benares
points: Gautama Buddha (563 B.C. – 483 B.C.) was Prince Siddhartha; after seeing a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession and a monk, he sought enlightenment and found it under the Bodhi Tree.
He preached his first sermon at Benares on the Ganges.
Kisa Gotami carries her dead son to neighbours asking for medicine and is sent to the Buddha, who asks for mustard seed from a house where no one has lost a loved one.
No such house exists; watching the city lights flicker and go out, she realises death is common to all and that she was selfish in her grief.
The Buddha says mortals, like ripe fruit and earthen vessels, are always in danger of death; grieving brings no peace, and one who draws out the arrow of lamentation obtains peace of mind.

sections.title: Thinking about the Text
points: What Kisa Gotami asks for the first and second time she goes from house to house, and whether she gets it.
What she understands the second time, why, and how the Buddha changed her understanding; whether she was 'selfish in her grief'.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise I rephrases old-fashioned words and phrases (give thee medicine for thy child, Pray tell me, repaired, kinsmen, Mark!) in current language.
Exercise II breaks a sentence joined with semicolons into three simple sentences and compares their rhythm.

sections.title: Speaking
points: Compare two recent texts on grief with the Buddha's sermon and discuss in groups whether his ideas still hold meaning.

sections.title: A Guide to Coping with the Death of a Loved One
points: The first text for the speaking task: grief is natural to all kinds of loss.
Common feelings include sadness, anger, guilt and self-reproach, anxiety, loneliness, fatigue and disbelief.
Helping grieving people means reaching out, being patient and letting them know you care.

subsections.title: Feelings of Grief
points: Lists the feelings and behaviours commonly experienced after the death of a loved one.

subsections.title: Helping Others Who Are Experiencing Grief
points: Advice on supporting a friend, loved one or co-worker who is grieving.

sections.title: Good Grief
points: The second text, by Amitai Etzioni, who lost his wife and later his son, says there is no set form or 'right' way to grieve.
Following the maxim 'We are not to ask why, but what', his family focus on what they can do for one another.

sections.title: Writing
points: Write a page on one of three topics: teaching someone a new or difficult idea, helping each other through difficult times, or thinking about oneself as unique or as one among billions.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes, with an extract from Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet and lines from Tagore to memorise.

subsections.title: Joy and Sorrow
points: The extract from The Prophet, saying joy and sorrow are inseparable.

sections.title: For Anne Gregory
points: A poem by William Butler Yeats, a conversation between a young man and a young woman about her yellow hair.
He says no young man will love her for herself alone rather than her hair; she says she can dye it; he replies that only God could love her for herself alone.

sections.title: Thinking about the Poem
points: What the 'great honey-coloured ramparts' are, why young men are 'thrown into despair', and why she would change her hair colour.
Qualities that make objects desirable, whether people can be loved 'for themselves alone', and whether a person can be separated from how they look.

keyTerms.meaning: a state of high spiritual knowledge
an area which is filled with deep sorrow
affected by suffering, disease or pain
the high, wide walls around a castle or fort

keyResults.label: Character: Gautama Buddha
keyResults.statement: Born Prince Siddhartha Gautama, he became 'the Awakened or the Enlightened' and preached his first sermon at Benares.

keyResults.label: Character: Kisa Gotami
keyResults.statement: A woman grieving for her only son who learns that death is common to all.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: Death is universal; peace of mind comes not from grieving but from overcoming sorrow and selfishness.

keyResults.label: Style
keyResults.statement: The text is written in an old-fashioned style ('give thee medicine for thy child', 'Pray tell me') and uses semicolons to combine clauses.

keyResults.label: Theme of 'For Anne Gregory'
keyResults.statement: Whether a person can be loved for themselves alone rather than for outward qualities such as beauty.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the picture headings Thinking about the Text, Thinking about Language, Speaking, Writing, In This Lesson and Thinking about the Poem, plus a pictured 'Glossary' heading. No writer is printed for the sermon; its source is given as '[Source: Betty Renshaw Values and Voices: A College Reader (1975)]', so author is null. The two grief texts are printed inside the Speaking task as 'I. A Guide to Coping with the Death of a Loved One' and 'II. Good Grief' (by Amitai Etzioni); 'Joy and Sorrow' is inside In This Lesson.

chapters.title: The Proposal
chapters.author: Anton Chekhov
chapters.overview: A one-act farce in which Ivan Lomov, a wealthy, nervous landowner, comes to ask for the hand of his neighbour Chubukov's daughter Natalya. Before he can propose, he and Natalya quarrel over who owns the Oxen Meadows, and Chubukov joins in with insults. When Natalya learns he came to propose, she has him fetched back, but they quarrel again over whose dog is better. Lomov faints, and Chubukov hastily joins their hands; the engagement is made, though the quarrelling continues.

sections.title: Before You Read
points: Activity: guessing what sort of proposal the play is about, reading about a Russian wedding and comparing Russian and Indian wedding customs.
Introduces the play as a farce written in 1888–89 about wealthy families seeking marriages that make good economic sense.

subsections.title: A Russian Wedding
points: An article on Russian wedding preparations, the groom answering questions to reach the bride, toasts, and the 'stealing' of the bride and her shoe.

subsections.title: Wedding Ceremonies in Russia and India
points: A table to fill with customs similar to and different from Indian ones.

sections.title: Characters
points: Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov, a landowner; Natalya Stepanovna, his daughter, twenty-five; Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov, a large, hearty but very suspicious neighbouring landowner.

sections.title: The Proposal
points: Lomov arrives in evening dress; Chubukov suspects he wants money but is delighted when he asks for Natalya's hand.
Alone, Lomov explains he is 35, suffers palpitations and must marry; Natalya enters and he begins a long preamble.
They quarrel over whether the Oxen Meadows are his or hers; Chubukov joins, and insults about each other's families fly until Lomov staggers out.
Learning Lomov came to propose, Natalya has hysterics and demands he be fetched; she concedes the Meadows are his.
They quarrel again over whether his dog Guess or their dog Squeezer is better; Lomov collapses and seems dead.
When he comes round, Chubukov puts his hand in Natalya's, they kiss and agree to marry — and immediately resume arguing about the dogs.

sections.title: Thinking about the Play
points: What Chubukov first suspects Lomov has come for, and whether he is sincere in welcoming him.
Whether Natalya is 'in love' as Chubukov claims.
Words and accusations the characters hurl at each other, adjectives to describe each character, and what they might quarrel about next.

sections.title: Thinking about Language
points: Exercise I looks at expressions that seem more Russian than English, the pronunciation and stress of words such as palpitations and pedigree, and phrases like 'My foot's gone to sleep'.
Exercise III rewrites a Times of India excerpt about A. K. Hangal, changing direct speech into reported speech.

subsections.title: Reported Speech
points: Explains reporting and reported clauses, with pairs of direct and reported sentences from the play, and the changes made in reporting.

sections.title: Speaking and Writing
points: Anger Management: the ill effects of anger and ways to avoid losing one's temper.
In pairs, a script from an excerpt of Tagore's The Home and the World.
In groups, qualities to look for in a marriage partner, and parts of the play resembling scenes from romantic comedies.

sections.title: In This Lesson
points: Teacher's notes: a dictation of biographical information for students to guess the playwright (Shakespeare, unnamed).

sections.title: Homophones
points: Words spelt alike with different meanings: close/close, present/present.

sections.title: Fundamental Rights
points: A page on the Constitution of India, Part III (Articles 12 – 35), listing the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.

keyTerms.meaning: the book describes the play as a one-act farce

keyResults.label: Character: Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov
keyResults.statement: A 35-year-old neighbouring landowner, large and hearty but very suspicious, who suffers palpitations and comes to propose.

keyResults.label: Character: Natalya Stepanovna
keyResults.statement: Chubukov's twenty-five-year-old daughter, a good housekeeper, who quarrels over the Meadows and the dogs.

keyResults.label: Character: Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov
keyResults.statement: A landowner and Natalya's father, who welcomes the proposal but joins every quarrel.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: Wealthy families seek marriages that make good economic sense; all three characters are quarrelsome over petty issues.

keyResults.label: Form
keyResults.statement: A one-act play, a farce, originally titled 'A Marriage Proposal', translated from the Russian.

chapters.notes: Read from the rendered page images: the picture headings Thinking about the Play, Thinking about Language, Speaking and Writing and In This Lesson. The byline under the title is printed 'Anton Chekov', while the introduction and the teacher's notes print 'Anton Chekhov'; the latter is used. 'Anger Management' is the italic label of the first Speaking and Writing task, not a heading, and is no longer a section. Reported Speech is exercise II of Thinking about Language. Page 21 carries the Constitution of India's Fundamental Rights, not part of the play.
